text: Orchestration is the layer that actually runs the variational loop against the real-world asynchronous job lifecycle: submitting, waiting, handling partial failure, and feeding results to the next classical step. This lesson builds that layer concretely.

A production orchestration layer owns far more than submit-and-wait: tracking job state across restarts, enforcing timeouts, deciding retry versus fail versus fallback, and logging cost and latency for every submission. We'll measure where time actually goes, and see how batching changes the shape of that time dramatically.

Here are real measured stage timings for one iteration. Classical prep, twelve milliseconds. Network round trips, a few hundred. Queue wait — thirty-eight thousand milliseconds, ninety-nine point one percent of the total. QPU execution itself is forty milliseconds. This single number should drive almost every orchestration decision you make — optimizing the twelve-millisecond classical step is not where the engineering effort belongs.

And here's where that gets built for real — Amazon Braket's Hybrid Jobs wizard, a genuine five-step flow for exactly this kind of batched, state-tracked submission. Submitting seventeen circuit evaluations as separate queued jobs versus one batched program set changes total wall-clock time by roughly seventeen times, because batching doesn't eliminate queue wait — it eliminates paying it over and over.

Here's Microsoft's own diagram of that same lifecycle, provider-agnostic: upload, queue, translate, process, return. A naive orchestration function that blocks in a loop ties up an entire process for the full queue wait. Production code instead models each job as an explicit state — pending, queued, running, done or failed — so one classical process can manage many in-flight quantum jobs concurrently.

Next lesson covers what happens when one of those jobs doesn't just sit in queue — it actually fails. A quantum cloud job can fail in more ways than a typical API call, and some of those failures still cost you money.
